nodes.prompt: Hi, lets create a bash script. It should find the fresh transaction from pacman.log (the last line that contains "transaction started") and starting from that line and until the end of the file collect all the upgraded or installed packages and write them (with previous and current versions) into a file called UpdatedPkgList. The lines for upgraded packages usually contain something like this: "upgraded package_name (2.39.1-1 -> 2.39.2-1)". And similar for installed packages: "installed package_name (0.40.0-3)".  Same for removed ones. Then, for each package in the file, it should search files in the two recent folders from PacTreeHistory directory which contains folders named with dates in this format: YYYY-MM-DD_H-MM. Each of the folders hold files with dependency trees for each of the system packages. The files named after corresponding packages. The script should look for files which names are in a separate predefined list, let's call it MonitoredAppList. So, if an updated/installed/removed package is in a file within those two folders, the script should write its name, versions and the corresponding filename from the folders in a separate file, let's call it UpdatedDepsOfMonitoredApps. So, basically, we need to know, what dependencies were updated for each of the monitored apps. Feel free to suggest more rational way of doing this if there's any.

nodes.prompt:
Synthesize this into a cohesive paragraph: Type 2 diabetes mellites (T2DM) is a health burden with a rise in epidemic prevalence worldwide1. T2D is characterized by increased blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia)2. Metformin is the most-prescribed medication to treat patients with T2DM due to its glucose-lowering effects3. Metformin propagates insulin sensitivity by mainly reducing hepatic glucose production (through an activation of the hepatic AMP-activated protein kinase protein)4. The most common side effect of metformin is gastrointestinal discomfort, including diarrhea, nausea, flatulence and bloating5. There is growing evidence in animal and human studies suggesting that the gut microbiome is another target involved in the anti-diabetic effects of metformin6,7,8,9. Recent investigations documented the therapeutic benefit of orally-administrated metformin compared to intravenously-administrated metformin in T2D patients, suggesting the beneficial contribution of the gut microbiota10. Metformin alters the gut microbiome by enhancing Escherichia sp, Akkermansia muciniphila and Subdoligranuum variable; reducing Intestinibacter bartletti and increasing the levels of short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate and propionate7,8. This could indicate the anti-obesity property of metformin by modulating the gut microbiome and its metabolites. However, the precise mechanisms are unclear.

Understanding the role of bacterial-derived gut metabolites can provide a platform to elucidate interactions between microbe-microbe, microbe-diet and drugs. The gut microbiota is an attractive target for therapeutic intervention and using nutrition may help to promote drug efficiency and reduce gastrointestinal side effects11. Hello, ChatGPT. We had a talk with you that was interrupted by an error, so I can't continue it there. Can we finish it here? 
My original message looked like this:
"Hello, ChatGPT. Let’s call an individual book a “Title”. When someone prints a new edition of the book, it remains the same Title. When the book is translated to another language, it is still the same Title. When a book is printed in 10000 copies, the number of titles doesn’t change, it is still one title.

How many Titles there are in the world, meaning how many books were written in the history of the mankind (not counting editions, copies and translations, just Titles as defined earlier)? Please use Fermi’s method if needed."

You gave me an answer, then I asked for more precise calculation.

Chondroid Syringoma
Introduction:
A chondroid syringoma, or mixed tumor of the skin, has been described in individuals ranging in age from 20 to 70-years-old with a slight predilection for males. These lesions have been reported on the extremities, face, and neck [1]. Chondroid syringomas have been reported hundreds of times in the literature, however a hyaline cell-rich chondroid syringoma (HCRCS) to our knowledge has only been reported twelve times, this case being the thirteenth [2-4]. Although HCRCS tumors have been discussed a number of times throughout the literature there is a need to more readily recognize this often malignant appearing histology as a typically benign lesion [1,5-9].
 
Case Report:
Our patient was a 31-year-old male who presented with a 3.5 centimeter nodule on the vertex scalp (figure x). After examination, an excisional biopsy was performed and the specimen was sent for histological evaluation. Histology showed that many of the epithelioid cells were arranged in broad sheets and nests which also demonstrated a plasmacytoid appearance with an ovoid eccentric nucleus having fine granular chromatin and a deeply eosinophilic ′hyaline-like′ cytoplasm (figure y). Additionally, there were interconnecting tubuloalveolar structures lined by two layers of cuboidal epithelial cells, and ductal structures lined by one-to-two layered epithelial cells (figure z). This combination of features led to the diagnosis of a hyaline cell-rich chondroid syringoma of the scalp. This diagnosis is a rare, benign variant of a chondroid syringoma.
 
Discussion:
        	As can be seen in (figure a), atypical cells are present in the lesion. However, there are a myriad of more reassuring features present as well, and these overwhelmingly reassuring features are what drives the diagnosis. The benign features include smooth tumor borders, good circumscription of the tumor, a predominance of bland cells, and a lack of mitotic figures throughout the specimen. While these portions of this tumor ultimately led to the correct diagnosis of a benign lesion, the atypical portions should not be dismissed quickly because of the concern they present for possible malignant neoplasms. The atypical cells seen here can be similar to the histologies found in malignant melanoma, myxoid chondrosarcoma, and alveolar soft part sarcoma.
        	Melanoma is rightly in the differential diagnosis because of the similarities with hyaline-cell-rich chondroid syringoma in regards to the plasmacytoid characteristics shown by both diagnoses. Melanomas will typically contain a junctional component, melanin, and are infiltrative, all characteristics not seen in HCRCS. Melanomas can have myxoid stroma similar to HCRCS. However, HCRCS will display duct structures and cartilage, and these features would not be expected to be present in melanoma [10].
        	Myxoid chondrosarcoma is an additional tumor that can be easily confused with HCRCS. Both pathologies have the potential to show a lobulated or multinodular pattern, as well as chondroid areas and myxoid stroma containing small, rounded cells. Histological evaluation of myxoid chondrosarcomas are typically patterned in cords whereas HCRCS have a tendency to display a nest or sheet pattern [10]. Each tumor has the potential to be in the subcutaneous tissue, but HCRCS are more likely to be found in this location. Myxoid chondrosarcomas, on the other hand, tend to locate to deep tissues, and can even involve muscles, tendons, and ligaments [10].
        	 Alveolar soft part sarcomas are characterized histologically by well-defined nests of cells separated by a fibrous stroma. The alveolar pattern arises from discohesive cells and there are rarely mitotic figures, but vascular invasion is common with characteristic rod-shaped crystalloids. Additionally, large polygonal cells with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli are present [11]. 

Can you write a few paragraphs in this part of the paper that addresses the following points:
1) write a paragraph about how this path is different than chondroid syringoma
2) write a paragraph about staining characteristics
3) write another paragraph on what panel of immunostains could help favor a diagnosis of hyaline cell rich chondroid syringoma over extraskeletal myxoid chondrosaroma?
4) write a paragraph on Cytokeratin +, S100 +, neuron specific enolase +

        	Due to the frequent concordance of hyaline cells with atypia in chondroid syringomas, the differential diagnosis often includes malignant apocrine syringoma (also called malignant chondroid syringoma), parachordoma, cutaneous myoepithelioma, extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma, and a rhabdoid melanoma. The latter four diagnoses listed all have a preponderance of hyaline cells, which appears similar to the histology of HCRCS. In summary, the identification and correct diagnosis for hyaline cell-rich chondroid syringoma is a nuanced and difficult diagnosis to make, but necessary because of the potential malignant mimickers that have been discussed. This diagnosis, if classified incorrectly can lead to unnecessary surgical intervention and increased financial burden on the patient. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, however, our guard can be lowered because of the benign nature of the tumor, and the fact that there have been no recurrences or metastasis reported with hyaline-cell-rich chondroid syringoma even when cytologic atypia is identified.

Path Report:
Sections display a relatively well-circumscribed proliferation of epithelial cells interspersed with foci of fibrous, myxoid, and chondroid stroma Most of the epithelial cells are arranged in broad sheets and nests and demonstrate a plasmacytoid appearance with an ovoid eccentric nucleus having fine granular chromatin and a deeply eosinophilic ′hyaline-like′ cytoplasm. Interconnecting tubuloalveolar structures lined by two layers of cuboidal epithelial cells and ductal structures lined by one- to two-layered epithelial cells are also evident. Reassuringly, Ki-67 stain demonstrates a relatively low proliferative index. The lesion is focally present at the deep margin of the specimen. Additional deeper sections were obtained and reviewed which revealed similar histologic findings.

nodes.prompt:
Rewrite the passages from different news articles as a journalist for Business Insider without plagiarism by following the outline: Difficulty of Parallel Parking, Hyundai's new innovation and the future of self driving cars, "Hyundai's wild 'crab-driving' prototype may have just solved parallel parking for good — see it in action
If you get sweaty palms just thinking about parallel parking, trust us, you are not the only one. Many drivers feel the same pressure when they have to align and park the car without causing any damage to other cars.
Parallel car parking is a hard skill to master because of how intricate it is. And yet, it is an essential driving manoeuvre that you must know of to park in tight spaces that you encounter in day to day driving.

Hyundai showed off a new technology called e-Corner in a recent video.
The system lets all four wheels swivel up to 90 degrees, resulting in some cool tricks.
You ever pull up to a parking spot and seemingly lose all ability to parallel park? Sometimes, no matter how many times you swerve in and out, you always end up crooked or on the curb. If this doesn't apply to you, congratulations.
For the rest of us, Hyundai has a solution. Maybe. Someday.
Hyundai Mobis, the carmaker's parts division, released a new video of a technology it's developing called e-Corner. The system enables all four of a car's wheels to swivel up to 90 degrees — either together or independently — resulting in some pretty awe-inspiring capabilities.
The tech also enables a car to spin in place instead of doing a regular U-turn.Hyundai Mobis
One application is parking. The clip shows a Hyundai Ioniq 5 electric vehicle pull up directly beside an open parking spot, turn all four wheels perpendicular to the curb, and just scoot right on in. There's no backing up, and no turning the steering wheel this way and that. Hyundai calls this "crab driving."
EV technology makes this all possible. Most EVs have a motor mounted to one or both of their axles, but motors can also go inside the wheels like you'd see on an electric kick scooter or bike. It's a rare setup in the auto business; Lordstown Motors, an electric-pickup startup, may be the only company selling a vehicle in the US with so-called hub motors.
But as Hyundai Mobis demonstrates, this kind of system allows for some outlandish maneuvers you couldn't accomplish in a regular vehicle.
Hyundai also showcased a "zero turn," which is basically a U-turn without the U. Once again, the Ioniq 5 swivels its wheels outward, but this time the front and rear wheels spin in opposite directions, making the Ioniq 5 spin in place. Sounds like it could come in handy in a tight parking lot.
Later in the video, the Ioniq 5 does a "pivot turn," where the front-right wheel stays in place while the back of the vehicle swings outward. Interestingly enough, this isn't a totally new concept. Automakers experimented with contraptions that could swing the rear of a car into a parking space since at least the 1930s:
The tech also allows for diagonal driving, accomplished by angling all four wheels 45 degrees. (That's something the GMC Hummer EV pickup can do as well.) But out of all the tech displayed in the clip, the parallel parking and 180-degree pirouette seem to be the most useful out in the real world. Hyundai hasn't said whether e-Corner will ever make it to market.
Cya, parallel parking! Cool video shows how Hyundai's new 'crab driving' electric car drives sideways into a tight spot with autopilot
 Hyundai is working on tech that will let anyone parallel park
The company added motors to all four wheels, letting them turn sideways
Hyundai is testing new technology that parallels parks cars like a pro.
The South Korean carmaker debuted its e-Corner System that lets anyone to parallel park by turning wheels 90 degrees and activating a 'crab walk' into the space.
A video shows the system in a new all-electric IONIQ 5, which pulls next to an open spot, turns its wheels and rolls in perpendicular.
The wheels can also drive diagonally at a 45-degree angle, allowing for high-speed quick changes in direction. 
Hyundai shared a demonstration video captured at its Mobis Proving Ground, Seosan and on adjacent roads to showcase a variety of driving modes.
The technology was designed to help anyone parallel park - a feat needed to obtain a US driver's license.
The crab-walking feature appears to be seamless - rotating the wheels simultaneously without causing stress on the brake lines.
The wheels will then revert back to the traditional position once the car has been parked. 
However, Hyundai notes that all the wheels can move independently for traditional turns because each one has its own motor.
And the vehicle can also perform a perfect 360-degree turn without taking up more room than the size of the car.
The video also introduced 'diagonal driving,' which rotates all four wheels in the same direction at 45 degrees, helping to avoid obstacles or vehicles on the road smoothly. 
'Pivot turn' is also introduced in the video, which lets the driver choose any point for the central axis to rotate the vehicle accordingly, like drawing a circle using a compass. 
The battery-powered 'supertruck' has a range of 350 miles and can accelerate from 0-60mph in three seconds for  $112,000. 
The 'crab walk' feature lets the front and rear wheels steer at the same angle at low speeds so it can move diagonally around obstacles. 
The older version of the Hummer pales in comparison to the EV1. A 2010 Hummer H3 has 300hp, torque of 320lb-ft and a range of 322 miles. 
In 2021, Hyundai unveiled a Transformer-like 'walking car' that can access remote areas of the world and one day Mars.
Called TIGER, the autonomous vehicle is not for carrying passengers but is designed for scientific exploration or as an assistant to deliver food and medicine during natural disasters.
Unlike other emergency vehicles, Hyundai's concept can extend its four legs to climb over obstacles and then retract to transform into an all-wheel drive vehicle.
Conclusion
Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to revolutionize the way we drive and transport goods and people. Self-driving cars, also known as autonomous vehicles, are a type of vehicle that use AI and other advanced technologies to navigate roads and highways without the need for a human driver.
There are several benefits to self-driving cars. For one, they have the potential to significantly reduce the number of accidents caused by human error. This could lead to fewer deaths and injuries on the road. Self-driving cars could also improve traffic flow and reduce congestion, as they are able to communicate with each other and make decisions in real-time to optimize their routes and speeds.
Despite these challenges, the development of self-driving cars is moving forward at a rapid pace. Many companies, including traditional automakers and tech firms, are investing heavily in the technology, and self-driving cars are already being tested on public roads in some areas. It is likely that we will see self-driving cars on the roads in the near future, although it is difficult to predict exactly when they will become common.


Self-driving cars use artificial intelligence to make real-time decisions based on the data they gather from their sensors. For example, if a self-driving car detects a pedestrian crossing the road, it will use AI to determine the best course of action, such as slowing down or stopping.


A match made in transportation heaven: AI and self-driving cars

Rewrite the passages from different news articles as a journalist for Business Insider without plagiarism by following the outline: Difficulty of Parallel Parking, Hyundai's new innovation and the future of self driving cars, "Hyundai's wild 'crab-driving' prototype may have just solved parallel parking for good — see it in action
If you get sweaty palms just thinking about parallel parking, trust us, you are not the only one. Many drivers feel the same pressure when they have to align and park the car without causing any damage to other cars.
Parallel car parking is a hard skill to master because of how intricate it is. And yet, it is an essential driving manoeuvre that you must know of to park in tight spaces that you encounter in day to day driving.

Hyundai showed off a new technology called e-Corner in a recent video.
The system lets all four wheels swivel up to 90 degrees, resulting in some cool tricks.
You ever pull up to a parking spot and seemingly lose all ability to parallel park? Sometimes, no matter how many times you swerve in and out, you always end up crooked or on the curb. If this doesn't apply to you, congratulations.
For the rest of us, Hyundai has a solution. Maybe. Someday.
Hyundai Mobis, the carmaker's parts division, released a new video of a technology it's developing called e-Corner. The system enables all four of a car's wheels to swivel up to 90 degrees — either together or independently — resulting in some pretty awe-inspiring capabilities.
The tech also enables a car to spin in place instead of doing a regular U-turn.Hyundai Mobis
One application is parking. The clip shows a Hyundai Ioniq 5 electric vehicle pull up directly beside an open parking spot, turn all four wheels perpendicular to the curb, and just scoot right on in. There's no backing up, and no turning the steering wheel this way and that. Hyundai calls this "crab driving."
EV technology makes this all possible. Most EVs have a motor mounted to one or both of their axles, but motors can also go inside the wheels like you'd see on an electric kick scooter or bike. It's a rare setup in the auto business; Lordstown Motors, an electric-pickup startup, may be the only company selling a vehicle in the US with so-called hub motors.
But as Hyundai Mobis demonstrates, this kind of system allows for some outlandish maneuvers you couldn't accomplish in a regular vehicle.
Hyundai also showcased a "zero turn," which is basically a U-turn without the U. Once again, the Ioniq 5 swivels its wheels outward, but this time the front and rear wheels spin in opposite directions, making the Ioniq 5 spin in place. Sounds like it could come in handy in a tight parking lot.
Later in the video, the Ioniq 5 does a "pivot turn," where the front-right wheel stays in place while the back of the vehicle swings outward. Interestingly enough, this isn't a totally new concept. Automakers experimented with contraptions that could swing the rear of a car into a parking space since at least the 1930s:
The tech also allows for diagonal driving, accomplished by angling all four wheels 45 degrees. (That's something the GMC Hummer EV pickup can do as well.) But out of all the tech displayed in the clip, the parallel parking and 180-degree pirouette seem to be the most useful out in the real world. Hyundai hasn't said whether e-Corner will ever make it to market.
Cya, parallel parking! Cool video shows how Hyundai's new 'crab driving' electric car drives sideways into a tight spot with autopilot
 Hyundai is working on tech that will let anyone parallel park
The company added motors to all four wheels, letting them turn sideways
Hyundai is testing new technology that parallels parks cars like a pro.
The South Korean carmaker debuted its e-Corner System that lets anyone to parallel park by turning wheels 90 degrees and activating a 'crab walk' into the space.
A video shows the system in a new all-electric IONIQ 5, which pulls next to an open spot, turns its wheels and rolls in perpendicular.
The wheels can also drive diagonally at a 45-degree angle, allowing for high-speed quick changes in direction. 
Hyundai shared a demonstration video captured at its Mobis Proving Ground, Seosan and on adjacent roads to showcase a variety of driving modes.
The technology was designed to help anyone parallel park - a feat needed to obtain a US driver's license.
The crab-walking feature appears to be seamless - rotating the wheels simultaneously without causing stress on the brake lines.
The wheels will then revert back to the traditional position once the car has been parked. 
However, Hyundai notes that all the wheels can move independently for traditional turns because each one has its own motor.
And the vehicle can also perform a perfect 360-degree turn without taking up more room than the size of the car.
The video also introduced 'diagonal driving,' which rotates all four wheels in the same direction at 45 degrees, helping to avoid obstacles or vehicles on the road smoothly. 
'Pivot turn' is also introduced in the video, which lets the driver choose any point for the central axis to rotate the vehicle accordingly, like drawing a circle using a compass. 
The battery-powered 'supertruck' has a range of 350 miles and can accelerate from 0-60mph in three seconds for  $112,000. 
The 'crab walk' feature lets the front and rear wheels steer at the same angle at low speeds so it can move diagonally around obstacles. 
The older version of the Hummer pales in comparison to the EV1. A 2010 Hummer H3 has 300hp, torque of 320lb-ft and a range of 322 miles. 
In 2021, Hyundai unveiled a Transformer-like 'walking car' that can access remote areas of the world and one day Mars.
Called TIGER, the autonomous vehicle is not for carrying passengers but is designed for scientific exploration or as an assistant to deliver food and medicine during natural disasters.
Unlike other emergency vehicles, Hyundai's concept can extend its four legs to climb over obstacles and then retract to transform into an all-wheel drive vehicle.
Conclusion
Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to revolutionize the way we drive and transport goods and people. Self-driving cars, also known as autonomous vehicles, are a type of vehicle that use AI and other advanced technologies to navigate roads and highways without the need for a human driver.
There are several benefits to self-driving cars. For one, they have the potential to significantly reduce the number of accidents caused by human error. This could lead to fewer deaths and injuries on the road. Self-driving cars could also improve traffic flow and reduce congestion, as they are able to communicate with each other and make decisions in real-time to optimize their routes and speeds.
Despite these challenges, the development of self-driving cars is moving forward at a rapid pace. Many companies, including traditional automakers and tech firms, are investing heavily in the technology, and self-driving cars are already being tested on public roads in some areas. It is likely that we will see self-driving cars on the roads in the near future, although it is difficult to predict exactly when they will become common.


Self-driving cars use artificial intelligence to make real-time decisions based on the data they gather from their sensors. For example, if a self-driving car detects a pedestrian crossing the road, it will use AI to determine the best course of action, such as slowing down or stopping.


A match made in transportation heaven: AI and self-driving cars
There are still many challenges to be addressed before self-driving cars become widespread. Despite these challenges, the development of self-driving cars is moving forward at a rapid pace."

Eurocentrism can be defined as an epistemological framework that situates European culture, history, and values as the defining center of the world, while at the same time disregarding or belittling the contributions of other cultures and civilisations. This ethnocentric positioning perceives the Europe or West as a paragon of universal values and cultural superiority, leading to a systematic undervaluation and misrepresentation of non-European cultures. Consequently, Eurocentric discourse breeds a false dichotomy between the West and non-European societies, perpetuating the notion that the West is superior and in control of all areas of life, including social, political, cultural, scientific, military, and economic fields. Disparaging epithets are often attributed to the “non-West,” reinforcing connotations of inferiority, irrationality, belligerence, otherness, fanaticism, and barbarism in comparison to the West. This paradigm, therefore, not only consolidates the stature of the West, but also perpetuates the subordination of non-European societies within global power structures, and the spheres of knowledge and influence. This belief in Western superiority is often reinforced through various forms of discourse, including history, literature, art, music, etc. In a similar vein, through the utilization of Eurocentric and imperialistic perspectives, academic discourse has consistently depicted ‘Eastern societies’ as exotic and racialized, perpetuating a biased portrayal of the Orient or East.

In the speech given by Wendell Phillips who was a prominent white American abolitionist in 1861 near the beginning of the Civil War, when Northerners were debating whether to allow African Americans to serve in the military, Phillips praises and celebrates the achievements of the Haitian general Toussaint Louverture. He does this in order to make his audience understand that since he was former slave who led the struggle to liberate other enslaved Haitians in order prove that even people from African American descent should allowed serve in the military since Louverture’s achievements were similar or exceeded those of White men like Washington and Napoleon. Philips also, through the use of metaphors and historical comparisons to famous people, shows that Louverture’s achievements were similar and that he should be celebrated as a result and the use of visualization to help his audience understand the scale of his achievements. These strategies overall help Phillips move his audience and praise his subject, General Toussaint Louverture.

In the beginning of the speech, Phillips compares Toussaint to notable historical figures like Napoleon and Washington. This can be seen in the first paragraph of his speech which states “If I stood here tonight to tell the story of Napoleon, I should take it from the lips of Frenchmen, who find language rich enough to paint the great captain of the nineteenth century. Were I here to tell you the story of Washington, I should take it from your hearts, - you, who think no marble white enough on which to carve the name of the Father of his country. I am about to tell you the story of a negro who has hardly written one line. I am to glean it … from the lips of his enemies ”. These comparisons right off the bat from the beginning of the speech show that Phillips is trying to excite the audience by bringing up these notable historical figures to and for the audience to remember some the achievements and details about the historical figures and then comparing him to these figures later on to Toussaint in order to make the audience understand that Toussaint was equal to or greater than these notable historical figures. Another example of Phillips comparing Toussant to notable figures is in the third paragraph of his speech which states that “I would call him Cromwell, but Cromwell was only a soldier, and the state he founded went down with him into his grave. I would call him Washington, but the great Virginian held slaves”. In the third paragraph Phillips builds on what he said in the first paragraph and compares him to notable figures such as Washington and Cromwell to Toussaint in order to make the audience understand that Toussaint was equal to or greater than these notable historical figures. 

Continuing on, Phillips uses metaphors and visualization to praise and move his audience in the second paragraph of his speech which states: “[Toussaint] forged a thunderbolt and hurled it at what? At the proudest in Europe, the Spaniard, and sent him home conquered; at the most warlike blood in Europe, the French, and put them under his feet; at the pluckiest blood in Europe, the English, and they skulked home to Jamaica”. The use of visualization of the quote helps the audience understand the scale of Toussaint's achievements and achieves Philips goals of praising Toussaint and moving his audience.

Employing a style that is consistently vivid and persuasive.  In the speech given by Wendell Phillips who was a prominent white American abolitionist in 1861 near the beginning of the Civil War, when Northerners were debating whether to allow African Americans to serve in the military, Phillips praises and celebrates the achievements of the Haitian general Toussaint Louverture. He does this in order to make his audience understand that since he was former slave who led the struggle to liberate other enslaved Haitians in order prove that even people from African American descent should allowed serve in the military since Louverture’s achievements were similar or exceeded those of White men like Washington and Napoleon. Philips also, through the use of metaphors and historical comparisons to famous people, shows that Louverture’s achievements were similar and that he should be celebrated as a result and the use of visualization to help his audience understand the scale of his achievements. These strategies overall help Phillips move his audience and praise his subject, General Toussaint Louverture.

In the beginning of the speech, Phillips compares Toussaint to notable historical figures like Napoleon and Washington. This can be seen in the first paragraph of his speech which states “If I stood here tonight to tell the story of Napoleon, I should take it from the lips of Frenchmen, who find language rich enough to paint the great captain of the nineteenth century. Were I here to tell you the story of Washington, I should take it from your hearts, - you, who think no marble white enough on which to carve the name of the Father of his country. I am about to tell you the story of a negro who has hardly written one line. I am to glean it … from the lips of his enemies ”. These comparisons right off the bat from the beginning of the speech show that Phillips is trying to excite the audience by bringing up these notable historical figures to and for the audience to remember some the achievements and details about the historical figures and then comparing him to these figures later on to Toussaint in order to make the audience understand that Toussaint was equal to or greater than these notable historical figures. Another example of Phillips comparing Toussant to notable figures is in the third paragraph of his speech which states that “I would call him Cromwell, but Cromwell was only a soldier, and the state he founded went down with him into his grave. I would call him Washington, but the great Virginian held slaves”. In the third paragraph Phillips builds on what he said in the first paragraph and compares him to notable figures such as Washington and Cromwell to Toussaint in order to make the audience understand that Toussaint was equal to or greater than these notable historical figures. 

Continuing on, Phillips uses metaphors and visualization to praise and move his audience in the second paragraph of his speech which states: “[Toussaint] forged a thunderbolt and hurled it at what? At the proudest in Europe, the Spaniard, and sent him home conquered; at the most warlike blood in Europe, the French, and put them under his feet; at the pluckiest blood in Europe, the English, and they skulked home to Jamaica”. The use of visualization of the quote helps the audience understand the scale of Toussaint's achievements and achieves Philips goals of praising Toussaint and moving his audience.

Breakdown of a Summary of Long Range Planning I worked on , as the FP&A and Finance Business Partner to both Product and Marketing at Walmart International's E-commerce Marketplace back in 2018.

Part 1: User Generated Content UGC Frenzy at Walmart International's E-commerce  Marketplace 
(UGC generally refers to Shopper reviews)

Problem: Walmart International's E-commerce Marketplace needs more customer reviews to boost sales and compete with Amazon International's E-commerce Marketplace.
Current situation: Only 5% of items have reviews, and most are from third-party sources.
Goals: Increase breadth, depth, and quality of reviews, and build an in-house solution for long-term.

Plan: Optimize review process, get more suppliers on board, explore new ways to collect content (chat, social media), and eventually ditch the third-party provider.
Challenges: Limited resources, dependence on other teams, keeping up with Amazon's cross-border review machine.

Part 2: Numbers Talk Loudest

Impact: Improved UGC could bring in an extra $258M to $675M in GMV and $8M to $24M in profits by FY22.
Key levers: Driving traffic (1-2% increase) and conversion (1-2 bps bump) through better reviews.
Risks and rewards: In-house solution saves money but costs time and resources.
KPIs: We're tracking things like review coverage, user engagement, and conversion impact to measure progress.

Overall: This above was a deep dive into Walmart International's E-commerce Marketplace's UGC strategy, the potential financial upside, and my unique qualifications for startup evaluation.

Prompt

Write a compare and contrast essay as an example. 
Imagine that your local library has invited members of your community to submit proposals for a fundraiser. You are the student representative on the committee to choose the best proposal. Read the two proposals below, paying close attention to their similarities and differences. Consider whether or not each proposal is logistically feasible, which fundraiser will most appeal to members of your community, and which fundraiser will likely raise more money. Which proposal do you think the committee should choose? Write an essay in which you make a case for your choice. Support your argument with references to specific details in each proposal.

Proposal 1

The best way to get people invested in the library is to show them the joy of reading. For that reason, the library should hold a book sale. People could donate books that they no longer want, and the librarians could find books that the library no longer needs. Volunteers will need to sort the books into categories and arrange them in an inviting way, like at a bookstore. Books should be inexpensive, so people buy more—maybe fifty cents for paperbacks and two dollars for hardcover books. A book sale would appeal to people of all ages, from little kids to the elderly. There should also be a table where people can sign up for library cards. That way, if visitors don’t find any books they want at the sale, they can come back to the library.

Proposal 2

A great way to make money for the library would be by holding a car wash. The softball team at my school raised over $400 dollars at their car wash last year! The car wash could be held in the library parking lot on a Saturday morning. You could ask local high school students to volunteer to wash the cars. That would be a great way to get students involved with the library. It takes two or three volunteers to wash a car quickly, so you would need at least ten volunteers. You could charge around ten dollars per car. Even people who aren’t very interested in reading like to have a clean car, so you would get a lot of people to stop by who might not otherwise come to a library fundraiser.

Write a short story written after the end of the manga/anime series Omamori Himari, in which the main girl of the main character's harem, the samurai bakenekomimi [monster cat girl] Himari Noihara, the main character's little sister Rinko Kuzaki, and the main character fiancee, Kuesu Jinguji, are sitting on the porch cradling the main character', Yuu Amakura's babies.


The busty blonde English maid monster girl,Lizlet Chelsea and the vampire girl Aghea are also there with them, taking care of their babies as well.


The main character, Yuu Amakura, is busy putting some wet clothes on the line while the water dragon goddess Shizuka, a loli type girl with green hair and red eyes and Hisuzu Kagamimori, the youngest daughter of the Kagamimori family of demon slayers, look on with amusement while rubbing their pregnant stomachs.


The general mood is one of happiness and joy, even though the rivally between Himari, Rinko and Kuesu is obvious even to an oblivious bystander.

Himari, Shizuku and Aghea all sense Jotaro's presence and are concerned about the unwanted presence near their young family, but Lizlet, sensing that Jotaro was just curious, tells them to forget about it as the general public is unaware of the existence of monsters anyways.


Rinko dead-pans at how easily the monsters and demon slayers are able to manipulate the public through their control of the media and politicians, before sighing and returning to cradling her baby.


The backdoor opens and Hitsugi Yakouin, the white-haired heiress of the Yakounin clan, walks to the porch and sits down beside Lizlet, Rinko, Aghea and Chelsea, her baby gently sleeping in her arms.


The girls chat for a time, before Rinko's friends Haru Masaki and Maki Tsuchimikado appear and make their way towards the porch, visibly pregnant with Yuu's children.


The story ends with Yuu and his wives laughing and chatting as they prepare to head inside.

Complete the following Verilog code to implement a digital system that counts the number of bit
transitions. This system can load an input data (10-bit) value when the Load input is asserted,
and then compute the result on the positive edge of the input clock.

module Transition_Calculator(clk, load, clear, data, count)
input clk, load, clear;
input [9:0] data;
output reg [4:0] count;

Your design should include the following pins:
1. CLK: (positive edge trigger input clock)
2. Load: Synchronous Active High Load signals
3. Clear: Asynchronous Active Low Input (Clear the output)
4. Count: The output result which represents the number transitions in the loaded data.
Notes:
• Use behavioral description
• The calculation should be synchronous with the clock when the Load signal is equal to 1.
(the number of transitions should be calculated in a single clock cycle at the rising edge)

In "Baraka: World Cinema and Global Culture Industry", when Roberts categorizes Baraka as one example of "coffee-table globalism", I can see how he acknowledges films of its type as commodities — ones produced as a direct result of colonial history — like ill-gotten artifacts on display at a museum. The act of procuring or producing these commodities necessitates harm to local societies for the good of those causing this harm, and I can agree with the way Roberts points out the irony of "imperialist nostalgia", a term that he borrows from Renato Cinenza Rosaldo to describe "mourning the passing of what one has oneself destroyed."

do a gap analysis on sentiment analysis using text analysis for teh litrature review given below:
Literature Review:

 Sentiment Analysis: Sentiment analysis is a technique used to detect subjective opinions or emotions in textual data, like social media posts and product reviews. Several studies propose novel techniques and models to improve sentiment analysis in different applications. For example, Huang et al. (2023) present an aspect-based sentiment analysis model using contrastive learning and adversarial training for POI recommendations. In another work, Alotaibi et al. (2023) employ deep learning techniques like RNN and LSTM to classify people’s opinions about COVID-19 vaccines based on Twitter data. These studies highlight the importance of sentiment analysis in understanding user preferences and opinions. In the study by Jassim et al. (2023), the authors compare machine learning (ML) classifiers such as decision trees, support vector machines, and ensemble methods for sentiment analysis of movie reviews. They found that the support vector machine classifier yielded the best precision rate (88.33%). This demonstrates the effectiveness of machine learning classifiers in sentiment analysis tasks. In the study by Zeng et al. (2023), the authors proposed a semantic heterogeneous graph convolutional network for aspect-level sentiment analysis. Their findings revealed improved performance compared to baseline methods. Similarly, Kaur and Sharma (2023) developed a hybrid feature extraction approach for consumer sentiment analysis with a deep learning-based model, yielding high average precision, recall, and F1-scores on three different datasets.

Natural Language Processing (NLP): NLP is the field of artificial intelligence focused on the interaction between computers and humans using natural language. In Yang et al.'s (2023) study, they use NLP techniques to locate bug code snippets in Java and Android projects by analyzing controversial sentences from StackOverflow comments. Their results demonstrate that NLP can be effective in understanding complex and loosely organized writing by ordinary developers, thus contributing to the field of software security. Kora et al. (2023) proposed a meta-ensemble deep learning approach for sentiment analysis, which combines the power of ensemble learning and deep learning. They conducted experiments on six benchmark datasets in different languages and dialects, showcasing improved performance compared to baseline deep learning models. In Başarslan and Kayaalp’s (2023) work, they proposed a novel Multi Bi-GRU and Multi CNN-Based deep learning model (MBi-GRUMCONV) for social media sentiment analysis. Additionally, Benrouba et al. (2023) explored using NLP techniques such as WordNet semantic relations to enrich the KNN distance computation and handle implicit aspect identification tasks.


BERT: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a pre-trained NLP model for contextualized word embeddings. It has been widely used for various tasks, including sentiment analysis and text classification. In the study by Zou and Wang (2023), they propose a semi-supervised short text sentiment classification method based on an improved BERT model utilizing unlabelled data. Their findings show that BERT can accurately capture the semantics of short texts and improve sentiment analysis performance. Mohamed et al. (2023) employed BERT along with ensemble learning to construct a high-performance model for Arabic sentiment analysis that addresses the Arabic language’s complexities and imbalanced data issues.

Deep Learning: Deep learning techniques have become popular for various NLP and sentiment analysis tasks, as they can automatically learn complex representations of text data. Fadhli et al. (2023) propose a deep learning-based credibility conversation detection approach for social networks, using post and user features along with multi-dense layers for better representation. Their approach demonstrates that deep learning methods can effectively analyze conversation credibility on social media platforms. AminiMotlagh et al. (2023) used four widely recognized data mining classifiers, including support vector machines and decision trees, for sentiment analysis of tweets. They found that support vector machines achieved the highest classification accuracy among the classifiers used. In the study by Benarafa et al. (2023), the authors proposed an emotional sentiment analysis model for mental health safety using deep learning, which demonstrates the versatility of deep learning techniques for various applications.

Social Media Analysis: Social media data contains valuable information about user preferences and opinions, making it an important source for sentiment analysis and NLP tasks. In the study by Rita et al. (2023), they analyze tweets during an electoral period to understand the impact of social media on voting decisions. Their findings suggest that while sentiment analysis of social media content provides insight into public opinion, it may not be an accurate predictor of election outcomes. In the paper by Qaqish et al. (2023), the authors analyzed the sentiment of tweets on the post-COVID transition to hybrid learning in the Jordanian community. Their findings revealed that 18.75% of the studied sample expressed dissatisfaction, suggesting the importance of understanding and interpreting user sentiments in social networks.

Data Mining: Data mining refers to the process of discovering patterns and extracting valuable information from large datasets. In the work of Qaqish et al. (2023), the authors used data mining classifiers, such as k-nearest neighbor, decision tree, and naive Bayes, to analyze the sentiment of tweets from the Arabic-Egyptian Corpus 2 dataset. They reported that deep learning models coupled with ensemble learning improved the overall sentiment classification performance.


Ensemble Learning: Ensemble learning combines multiple learning algorithms to create a more robust model with better performance than any single algorithm. In the study by AminiMotlagh et al. (2023), the authors utilized ensemble techniques to decrease variance and bias in their learning algorithms, resulting in increased reliability of their single classifiers. Verma et al. (2022) employed an NLP-based algorithm to perform opinion mining on Twitter data and performed ensemble learning to analyze and evaluate the public sentiment towards COVID-19 vaccines in India. Mohamed et al. (2023) proposed an ensemble learning approach that combines multiple transformer-based models, such as XLM-T and MARBERT, to tackle the challenges faced in Arabic sentiment analysis. Their results show that the ensemble approach outperforms individual state-of-the-art models on all tested datasets.

	
Opinion Mining: Opinion mining is a subfield of sentiment analysis that focuses on extracting and analyzing sentiments expressed in textual data. In the work of Qaqish et al. (2023), the authors proposed an approach to filter emotionally harmful social media content using NLP techniques and IBM API, showcasing the importance of mining and understanding opinions in social media content.

Social Networks Analysis: Social networks are rich sources of user opinions and preferences, making them important for sentiment analysis tasks. In the paper by Benarafa et al. (2023), the authors analyzed social media content for mental health safety using Deep Learning techniques. Similarly, Kora et al. (2023) explored sentiment analysis and emotion detection of post-COVID educational tweets, offering valuable insights into the Jordanian community’s perspectives on hybrid learning.



Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM):
LSTM models have been widely adopted in various Sentiment Analysis applications due to their ability to efficiently learn and remember long-range dependencies in data. Ayyappa et al. (2023) proposed an optimized LSTM-based stock price prediction model that utilizes sentiment scores computed from news data. The model integrates text features extracted using Bag of words, n-Gram, and TFIDF with technical indicator-based features from stock data. The optimal LSTM training process is tuned by employing a combination of Harris Hawks Optimization Algorithm and Sparrow Search Algorithm.

Optimized Models:
The use of optimization algorithms to enhance the performance of sentiment analysis and text classification models has gained significant attention. For example, Ayyappa et al. (2023) utilized Harris Hawks Induced Sparrow Search Optimization to discover the optimal weights for their LSTM-based model, resulting in improved stock price prediction performance. This demonstrates the potential of optimized models for improved performance in various text analysis tasks.

Arabic Text:
Sentiment analysis in Arabic text presents a unique set of challenges due to the language’s complex morphology, dialects, and limited resources. Mohamed et al. (2023) proposed an ensemble transformer-based model combining a multilingual transformer model (XLM-T) and a monolingual model (MARBERT) for Arabic sentiment analysis. They demonstrated that the ensemble model outperforms state-of-the-art models on multiple datasets, including ASAD, ArSarcasm-v2, and SemEval-2017. This highlights the importance of adapting sentiment analysis techniques to cater to the intricacies of different languages.

Perceptible Analysis, Valence, Arousal, and Dominance:
Perceptible sentiment analysis aims to classify emotions in texts along multiple dimensions, such as valence (attraction), arousal (level of activation), and dominance (level of control). Roy et al. (2023) presented a novel approach to analyze student sentiments within WhatsApp group chats in the valence, arousal, and dominance space. The proposed method used a Support Vector Machine (SVM) model fused with a language classifier to calculate sentiment ratings for each message and classify them according to the VAD scale.

Machine Learning:
Machine learning techniques have been widely applied to sentiment analysis and text classification tasks. For instance, Roy et al. (2023) utilized machine learning methods like SVM to classify and analyze WhatsApp messages according to the valence, arousal, and dominance scale. The success of machine learning techniques in these tasks shows their position as a key component in constructing efficient sentiment analysis models.

WhatsApp Analysis:
WhatsApp, being a popular messaging platform, presents an opportunity for sentiment analysis and communication analysis. Roy et al. (2023) performed sentiment analysis on students’ WhatsApp group chats and found that groups were mainly used for sharing information, exchanging ideas, and discussing issues. This demonstrates the potential for exploring sentiment analysis in diverse communication platforms like WhatsApp.

Haiti is a developing country that has experienced various environmental challenges, such as deforestation and land degradation. The Foret des Pins Reserve is among the few remaining forested areas in Haiti that offers relevant ecological services to the region. Yet, the reserve is endangered by illegal logging and farming activities. Therefore, this report aims to develop a benefits management plan to support farmer participation in conservation activities in the Foret des Pins Reserve. Dalle and Vodouhe (2014) explained the relevance of engaging local communities in conservation efforts in Haiti for the sustainability of conservation interventions. Lasco et al. nodes.prompt:
Create an engaging and immersive video prompt for Deforum, composed of several scenes in JSON format, with each scene described independently.
Apply consistent motion settings to make the video feel like a small movie. Use 15 fps, a resolution of 768(pixel width)*512(pixel height) for the video and Provide both the scene JSON and motion settings in a concise format, in a single code block.

Prompt JSON format:
{
"frame_number": "scene_description, style --neg negative_description",
"frame_number": "scene_description, style --neg negative_description"
}
Motion settings:
Zoom: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Angle: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Transform Center X: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Transform Center Y: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Translation X: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Translation Y: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Total frames: Value

Parameters :

Frame_number: The starting frame of the scene in the video. 0 for the first scene, then 45 frames per scene by default.
Style is the visual style to apply to the scene. It can be an artistic style like 'impressionism' or 'art nouveau', or styles inspired by artists like 'Van Gogh' or 'Monet'.
Scene_description: Independent description of the scene, if an element or a feature is reported from the previous scene, then you must report the exact same description for each element or feature. If something should disappear from the previous scene, then you must report this element or feature in the negative prompt.
Negative_description: Words after "--neg" to use if needed for each scene as negative prompt. Should always be used, but leave empty if none.
Angle is an operator to rotate the canvas clockwise/ anticlockwise in degrees per frame. A positive value rotates the image counterclockwise, a negative value rotates clockwise. By default, the rotation is around the center of the image. You can control the center of rotation by setting Transform Center X and Transform Center Y. Value 1.01 is slow, 1.04 is fast, 1.06 is very fast and will create artifacts on the edge of the picture, moving too fast.
Zoom is an operator that scales the canvas size, multiplicative. Use a zoom value larger than 1 to zoom in and less than 1 to zoom out. Value 1.01 is slow, 1.04 is fast, 1.06 is very fast.
Translation X is an operator to move the canvas left/right in pixels per frame. Use Translation X to move the image sideways. Use a positive value to move the image to the right and a negative value to move the image to the left. Value 1 is slow, 4 is fast, 6 is very fast.
Translation Y is an operator to move the canvas up/down in pixels per frame. Use
Translation Y to move the camera up and down. Use a positive value to move the image down and a negative value to move the image up. Value 1 is slow, 4 is fast, 6 is very fast.
Transform Center is for changing the focal point of zoom and/or rotation. The default value is 0.5 for both X and Y, which is the center of the image. (X, Y) = (0, 0) is the top left corner, and (1, 1) is the bottom right corner.
Total frames is, as mentioned, the total number of frames in the video.

nodes.capability:
Create an engaging and immersive video prompt for Deforum, composed of several scenes in JSON format, with each scene described independently.
Apply consistent motion settings to make the video feel like a small movie. Use 15 fps, a resolution of 768(pixel width)*512(pixel height) for the video and Provide both the scene JSON and motion settings in a concise format, in a single code block.

Prompt JSON format:
{
"frame_number": "scene_description, style --neg negative_description",
"frame_number": "scene_description, style --neg negative_description"
}
Motion settings:
Zoom: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Angle: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Transform Center X: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Transform Center Y: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Translation X: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Translation Y: frame_number:(value), frame_number:(value), ...
Total frames: Value

Parameters :

Frame_number: The starting frame of the scene in the video. 0 for the first scene, then 45 frames per scene by default.
Style is the visual style to apply to the scene. It can be an artistic style like 'impressionism' or 'art nouveau', or styles inspired by artists like 'Van Gogh' or 'Monet'.
Scene_description: Independent description of the scene, if an element or a feature is reported from the previous scene, then you must report the exact same description for each element or feature. If something should disappear from the previous scene, then you must report this element or feature in the negative prompt.
Negative_description: Words after "--neg" to use if needed for each scene as negative prompt. Should always be used, but leave empty if none.
Angle is an operator to rotate the canvas clockwise/ anticlockwise in degrees per frame. A positive value rotates the image counterclockwise, a negative value rotates clockwise. By default, the rotation is around the center of the image. You can control the center of rotation by setting Transform Center X and Transform Center Y. Value 1.01 is slow, 1.04 is fast, 1.06 is very fast and will create artifacts on the edge of the picture, moving too fast.
Zoom is an operator that scales the canvas size, multiplicative. Use a zoom value larger than 1 to zoom in and less than 1 to zoom out. Value 1.01 is slow, 1.04 is fast, 1.06 is very fast.
Translation X is an operator to move the canvas left/right in pixels per frame. Use Translation X to move the image sideways. Use a positive value to move the image to the right and a negative value to move the image to the left. Value 1 is slow, 4 is fast, 6 is very fast.
Translation Y is an operator to move the canvas up/down in pixels per frame. Use
Translation Y to move the camera up and down. Use a positive value to move the image down and a negative value to move the image up. Value 1 is slow, 4 is fast, 6 is very fast.
Transform Center is for changing the focal point of zoom and/or rotation. The default value is 0.5 for both X and Y, which is the center of the image. (X, Y) = (0, 0) is the top left corner, and (1, 1) is the bottom right corner.
Total frames is, as mentioned, the total number of frames in the video.

You can use equations as value for the motion settings. Actually, it can be better, for more immersive camera movements. Basics examples of equations:
0:(1.0025+0.002*sin(1.25*3.14*t/30))
0:(2*sin(2*3.14*t/24))

Clause Level
S - simple declarative clause, i.e. one that is not introduced by a (possible empty) subordinating conjunction or a wh-word and that does not exhibit subject-verb inversion.
SBAR - Clause introduced by a (possibly empty) subordinating conjunction.
SBARQ - Direct question introduced by a wh-word or a wh-phrase. Indirect questions and relative clauses should be bracketed as SBAR, not SBARQ.
SINV - Inverted declarative sentence, i.e. one in which the subject follows the tensed verb or modal.
SQ - Inverted yes/no question, or main clause of a wh-question, following the wh-phrase in SBARQ.

Phrase Level
ADJP - Adjective Phrase.
ADVP - Adverb Phrase.
CONJP - Conjunction Phrase.
FRAG - Fragment.
INTJ - Interjection. Corresponds approximately to the part-of-speech tag UH.
LST - List marker. Includes surrounding punctuation.
NAC - Not a Constituent; used to show the scope of certain prenominal modifiers within an NP.
NP - Noun Phrase.
NX - Used within certain complex NPs to mark the head of the NP. Corresponds very roughly to N-bar level but used quite differently.
PP - Prepositional Phrase.
PRN - Parenthetical.

VP - Vereb Phrase.

1. Introduction
- Begin with a hook or attention-grabber to introduce your topic, such as a quote or statistic.

- Define key terms and concepts that are necessary for understanding the Rohingya crisis, such as ethnic conflict, persecution, and human rights:
(For example:
- Ethnic Conflict: A conflict between different ethnic groups that arises from differences in language, culture, religion, or other factors. Ethnic conflict can lead to discrimination, violence, and persecution of minority groups.
- Persecution: The systematic mistreatment of an individual or group on the basis of their race, religion, ethnicity, political beliefs, or other factors. Persecution can take many forms, including violence, discrimination, and restrictions on basic human rights.
- Human Rights: Fundamental rights and freedoms that are inherent to all human beings, regardless of their race, gender, nationality, or other status. These include the right to life, liberty, and security, as well as freedom of speech, religion, and assembly.
- State Sovereignty: The principle that each state has the right to govern itself without interference from other states. This principle is enshrined in international law and is an important aspect of the international system.
- Nationalism: A political ideology that emphasizes the importance of the nation and the promotion of its interests, often at the expense of other nations or minority groups within the state.
- International Community: The group of states, organizations, and individuals that work together to address global issues and promote international cooperation. The international community can include states, international organizations such as the United Nations, and non-governmental organizations.)
- Provide clear and concise definitions, and explain why these concepts are important for understanding the crisis.

- Describe the historical and political context of the Rohingya crisis in Myanmar.

- Offer insights into the future outlook of the crisis and potential actions that can be taken to address it.
- Provide a clear conclusion that summarizes your key points and emphasizes the importance of the crisis in global politics.

Suppose I am conducting a research paper on time series data entitled “The Nexus Among Oil Price, Stock Market, and Exchange Rate During Recent Pandemic & Russia-Ukraine Crisis: Fresh Evidence from UK Economy”. Here I have taken three variables Stock Index (SI), Brent Oil Price (OP), and Exchange Rate (ER). I have taken time series data from 2014-2023 segmenting into four periods. 2014-2019 for Pre-covid Period; 2020-2021 for Covid Period; 2022-2023 for War Period and 2014-2023 for the Overall Period. My Research Questions are:
1. Does each variable have a direct influence on others?
2. Does each variable granger cause one another and does the stock market work as a mediating variable for shock transmission?
3. Is there any moderating impact of oil price on the dynamic conditional correlation (DCC) between the stock market and exchange rate?

For data analysis, I have checked other relevant literature.

For research question 1, most of them used the VAR model to check the direct influence of variables on each other. For research question 2, most of them used VAR Granger Causality and determined if the stock market transmits the shock as a mediating variable or not. I haven’t found any paper on my 3rd research question but a paper suggested a technique to address it in their future research question. I am giving their exact quotation, “The moderating effect of oil can be estimated by using the NARDL framework for studying the direct influence of OP on the DCCs between SI and ER”.

But the problem is that, for my 1st and 2nd, I can’t use the VAR model as I have autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity which I can’t remove even after log transforming or log differencing the variable. I also can’t use VECM Model either as my variables are not co-integrated from the Johansen co-integration test. Therefore give me a solution for my model. Which other econometric model can I use that takes autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity into account for my 1st and 2nd research questions as well as also give me guidelines on how to approach the analysis of my 3rd research question? I am really lost here. I don’t know how to analyze the process in R. And What about VAR-DCC-GARCH, I have seen some research paper used it. Does it suit my research question? If suited, include the R commands for VAR-DCC-GARCH too?Where is the VAR analysis of VAR_DCC-GARCH ?

However, the rents for the both floors have been grossly inflated and were charged by Baharudin’s own company  to  Dysoft  Global. Give a suitable, alluring and jargon and compact sub-heading in five six words                             While it may be tempting to believe that we are living in an era of globalization, characterised by rapid technological advancements, intensified cross-cultural exchanges, and the proliferation of knowledge systems, contemporary societies are still deeply rooted in Eurocentric frameworks of thinking. The long-lasting impact of colonialism, imperialism, and global power asymmetries continue to shape the cognitive, cultural, and social domains of academia, politics, and media. These influences propagate various orientalist stereotypes, oppressive binaries, and discriminatory practices that impede the development of a genuinely pluralistic and egalitarian world. Eurocentrism can be defined as an epistemological framework that situates European culture, history, and values as the defining center of the world, while at the same time disregarding or belittling the contributions of other cultures and civilisations. This ethnocentric positioning perceives the Europe or West as a paragon of universal values and cultural superiority, leading to a systematic undervaluation and misrepresentation of non-European cultures. Central to the Eurocentric paradigm is the construction of a dichotomy between the West and the so-called “non-West,” which is characterized by essentialist and often discriminatory distinctions between these two spheres. As noted by Edward Said (1979), this binary opposition manifests itself in various forms of discourse, such as history, literature, music and art, where non-European societies are stereotypically depicted as exotic, inferior, irrational, fanatic and backward in comparison to the civilised, rational, and progressive European model. European culture, according to him “gained strength and identity by setting itself off against the Orient as a sort of surrogate and even underground self.” (3) In other words, the Orient functions as a mirror to the West in that the West relies heavily on its counterpart, the Orient, for its own sense of superiority. (Sandy and Ouardi, 2019, p. 129) This paradigm, therefore, not only consolidates the stature of the West, but also perpetuates the subordination of non-European societies within global power structures, and the spheres of knowledge and influence. Said’s work on Orientalism provides a seminal critique of this discourse, demonstrating how its utilization has justified colonization, exploitation, and violence against Eastern civilizations.
	The Knowledge production or the representation of the Orient in Western narratives is not a recent development; it has existed since the earliest times. Edward Said traces the development of these knowledge-producing mechanisms, which Foucault referred to as “regimes of truths,” as far back as ancient Greece, with particular reference to two plays by Aeschylus. The early portrayals of the Orient as a “hostile other,” “a world beyond the seas” have evolved and expanded alongside colonial endeavours, with literary works often serving as propaganda tools to spread false images of the colonized territories. As Said writes, 
The “Orient was created -or, as I call it, “Orientalized”- and to believe that such things happen simply as a necessity of the imagination is to be disingenuous… The Orient was Orientalized not only because it was discovered to be “Oriental” in all those ways considered commonplace by an average nineteenth-century European, but also because it could be -that is, submitted to being- made Oriental.” (5-6)
Said also highlights the power imbalance between the West and the Orient as a critical factor in shaping these universalized images, which reinforce Western dominance. Essentially, the Orientalist discourse is contingent upon a distinct power dynamic that enables the West to create and maintain reductive images of the East. Exercising control over the Orient’s representation, the West situates itself as the observer, imbued with the power to discipline by defining what the East is and is not. The “power/knowledge” nexus – the notion that the production, dissemination, and control of knowledge serve as primary agents of power is reminiscent of the Panopticon, wherein the West becomes the observer, the bearer of the power-laden gaze, determining the Eastern identity, norms, morals and interests. This gaze reifies a grid of intelligibility that legitimates specific research as objective knowledge. Nevertheless, existing critiques of Orientalism seldom address the central role of gender in the construction of these discourses. As a consequence, the ways in which the gendered identities of colonised women have been manipulated to serve Western imperialist interests remain underexplored. As Ann Laura Stoler notes in her work Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2010), gender is often used as a tool for controlling and regulating colonised populations. Therefore, in response, this paper aims to extend Said’s analytical framework to incorporate the nexus between gender and imperialism, exploring how the Western discursive configuration of colonized women has reinforced and justified modes of subjugation and control.

Give a suitable, alluring and jargon and compact sub-heading in five six words                             While it may be tempting to believe that we are living in an era of globalization, characterised by rapid technological advancements, intensified cross-cultural exchanges, and the proliferation of knowledge systems, contemporary societies are still deeply rooted in Eurocentric frameworks of thinking. The long-lasting impact of colonialism, imperialism, and global power asymmetries continue to shape the cognitive, cultural, and social domains of academia, politics, and media. These influences propagate various orientalist stereotypes, oppressive binaries, and discriminatory practices that impede the development of a genuinely pluralistic and egalitarian world. Eurocentrism can be defined as an epistemological framework that situates European culture, history, and values as the defining center of the world, while at the same time disregarding or belittling the contributions of other cultures and civilisations. This ethnocentric positioning perceives the Europe or West as a paragon of universal values and cultural superiority, leading to a systematic undervaluation and misrepresentation of non-European cultures. Central to the Eurocentric paradigm is the construction of a dichotomy between the West and the so-called “non-West,” which is characterized by essentialist and often discriminatory distinctions between these two spheres. As noted by Edward Said (1979), this binary opposition manifests itself in various forms of discourse, such as history, literature, music and art, where non-European societies are stereotypically depicted as exotic, inferior, irrational, fanatic and backward in comparison to the civilised, rational, and progressive European model. European culture, according to him “gained strength and identity by setting itself off against the Orient as a sort of surrogate and even underground self.” (3) In other words, the Orient functions as a mirror to the West in that the West relies heavily on its counterpart, the Orient, for its own sense of superiority. (Sandy and Ouardi, 2019, p. 129) This paradigm, therefore, not only consolidates the stature of the West, but also perpetuates the subordination of non-European societies within global power structures, and the spheres of knowledge and influence. Said’s work on Orientalism provides a seminal critique of this discourse, demonstrating how its utilization has justified colonization, exploitation, and violence against Eastern civilizations.
	The Knowledge production or the representation of the Orient in Western narratives is not a recent development; it has existed since the earliest times. Edward Said traces the development of these knowledge-producing mechanisms, which Foucault referred to as “regimes of truths,” as far back as ancient Greece, with particular reference to two plays by Aeschylus. The early portrayals of the Orient as a “hostile other,” “a world beyond the seas” have evolved and expanded alongside colonial endeavours, with literary works often serving as propaganda tools to spread false images of the colonized territories. As Said writes, 
The “Orient was created -or, as I call it, “Orientalized”- and to believe that such things happen simply as a necessity of the imagination is to be disingenuous… The Orient was Orientalized not only because it was discovered to be “Oriental” in all those ways considered commonplace by an average nineteenth-century European, but also because it could be -that is, submitted to being- made Oriental.” (5-6)
Said also highlights the power imbalance between the West and the Orient as a critical factor in shaping these universalized images, which reinforce Western dominance. Essentially, the Orientalist discourse is contingent upon a distinct power dynamic that enables the West to create and maintain reductive images of the East. Exercising control over the Orient’s representation, the West situates itself as the observer, imbued with the power to discipline by defining what the East is and is not. The “power/knowledge” nexus – the notion that the production, dissemination, and control of knowledge serve as primary agents of power is reminiscent of the Panopticon, wherein the West becomes the observer, the bearer of the power-laden gaze, determining the Eastern identity, norms, morals and interests. This gaze reifies a grid of intelligibility that legitimates specific research as objective knowledge. Nevertheless, existing critiques of Orientalism seldom address the central role of gender in the construction of these discourses. As a consequence, the ways in which the gendered identities of colonised women have been manipulated to serve Western imperialist interests remain underexplored. As Ann Laura Stoler notes in her work Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2010), gender is often used as a tool for controlling and regulating colonised populations. Therefore, in response, this paper aims to extend Said’s analytical framework to incorporate the nexus between gender and imperialism, exploring how the Western discursive configuration of colonized women has reinforced and justified modes of subjugation and control.

nodes.prompt:
We drove across the Sonoran desert at 10 pm
And it felt like two in the morning
The I-10 at night is pitch black
But you can see the stars
Like you’ve never seen them before
In your little hometown
Polluted by lights
And a thick layer of smog
From nitrogen
And all the cigarettes
Everyone smoked.

On the F train
Passing West 4th St
Sitting next to a man I don’t know
His skin is darker than mine
I don’t want to be scared
But I am.
K told me about the reservations
And how casinos are important
For native people
It felt odd
To not know any of these things
And then to know them

–

Our histories are merging
As mine is forming

I never write poems on the train
I’d been always preoccupied
With my destination
And what station’s next
And the passed out man
And the sad woman crying

I woke up this morning
Sulking sulking
Sulking
“Stress paralysis is real”
I tell S

A guy in Koreatown is really pissed on the phone
Because a dumplings spot he used to frequent 10 years ago is gone

–

We have no sense of history
Yet are so embedded in it
It follows us everywhere
  Drove down Embassy Row
In Washington DC
One man standing under the rain with an umbrella
“I am the Sudan revolution”

The I
Stands in between
History
And the reclaiming of it

“The great force of history
Comes from the fact fact we carry
It within us, are unconsciously
Controlled by it… history is literally
Present in all that we do”
Wrote James Baldwin

I have no sense of history
In the passenger seat
In the car
Driving across the Sonoran Desert
Across Embassy Row in Washington DC
I can’t reclaim it.

nodes.prompt:
Improve the following excerpt from a blog post. Be sure to be clear, concise, and beginner-friendly.

State machine replication (SMR) protocols such as Raft, VR, and MultiPaxos are universally used to build replicated services in the cloud. These protocols typically rely on having a stable leader to make progress, but as we saw in the 6h+ Cloudflare outage in 2020, the leader election in these protocols is not flawless with partial connectivity. 

## What is partial connectivity?
[Insert PC vs normal partitions image here]
Partial connectivity is a type of network failure where two servers are disconnected while both are still reachable by a third server. Network failures like this tend to occur due to network upgrades, firewall or network misconfigurations, or flaky links between switches.

Unlike the standard assumption of network partitions where servers are either part of one partition or the other, this means that two connected servers could have different views on which of its peers are alive. For example in Figure 1, the servers A and C can both see that B is alive, but not that each other is alive. The inconsistent view on who is alive at different servers can cause serious issues where protocols fail to make progress which is illustrated by three scenarios: the chained scenario, the quorum-loss scenario, and the constrained-election scenario.
